 caret-right News | Space NASA’s Voyager 1 hits record one light-day distance, 50 years after launch
 Voyager 1 reaches one light-day from Earth, marking a historic milestone nearly 50 years after its 1977 launch.

 facebook x whatsapp-stroke copylink google Add Al Jazeera on Google info An undated artist's concept shows NASA's Voyager 1 spacecraft [File: Reuters via NASA] By Al Jazeera Staff and AFP Published On 18 Nov 2026 18 Nov 2026 NASA’s Voyager 1 probe, the most distant human-made object, has reached a distance of one light-day from Earth nearly 50 years after it was launched.
 The spacecraft hit the milestone on Wednesday and is now about 26 billion km away, according to NASA.

 end of list A light-day is the distance light can travel in 24 hours, which means messages sent from Earth take a day to reach Voyager 1, and another day for teams on the ground to receive a reply.
 The feat is “the best illustration of just how vast space is”, said NASA scientist Tiffany Kataria. “So much of what we dream about is travelling to other stellar systems,” she told the AFP news agency. “And it took Voyager 1 nearly 50 years to get to just the edge of our own solar system, let alone to only a light-day.”
 Many exoplanetary systems, she noted, are at least several light-years away. NASA expects Voyager 1 to take about 18,000 years to travel a full light-year.
 Interstellar space
 Launched in 1977, Voyager 1 and its twin Voyager 2 are the only spacecraft to have reached interstellar space, the region beyond the Sun’s heliosphere. Voyager 2 is expected to reach one light-day in 2035.
 Some of Voyager 1’s equipment, including its cameras, has been switched off remotely to save power, but the probe continues to study invisible phenomena such as magnetic fields.
 The data helps researchers study “the gas, the dust and other material that exists between stars”, Kataria said.
 Both craft carry “Golden Records”, 30cm gold-plated copper discs intended to convey the story of our world to extraterrestrials.
 Advertisement Earlier in their journeys, the Voyagers explored the giant planets Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune.
 Images of Jupiter taken by Voyager 1 first revealed the existence of rings around the planet and helped scientists understand the “really extreme vortices and weather” in its atmosphere, Kataria added.
